newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to propose $43 million for food safety.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to propose $43 million for food safety.

text.p: President Clinton plans to propose a $43 million programme to improve food safety in the United States, including an early warning sytem for food-borne illnesses and a significant boost in funding for seafood inspection, the White House said Friday.

"The president will be announcing a system that will help catch and respond to outbreaks of food-borne illness earlier and to help give us the data to prevent future outbreaks," said a White House spokeswoman, Mary Ellen Glynn.
She said Clinton planned to unveil details of his food safety proposal for the fiscal 1998 budget in his weekly radio address, to be broadcast Saturday.

Glynn said Clinton would propose a $43 million increase in food safety funding, which would include an $11.5 million food early-warning system for illnesses attributed to food. Another $10 million would go to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta to keep track of data on food-borne illnesses and $1 million for the Food and Drug Administration.
The remainder, more than $20 million, would go to the FDA for seafood safety inspection, including research, risk assessment and education, she said.
Food and consumer groups welcomed the news.

"This is a badly needed shot in the arm for the FDA -- they have suffered under tremendous funding deficiencies for food safety inspections," said Caroloyn Smith De Waal of the Centre for Science in the Public Interest.

The Agriculture Department is responsible for inspecting meat and poultry, but the job of overseeing the safety of the millions of pounds of seafood Americans eat every year falls to the FDA. Consumer activists have long complained of an inadequate seafood inspection system due to lack of funding.

"Agriculture Department inspectors are in meat and poultry plants every single day, but the FDA is in seafood plants at best once a year, and at worst maybe only once every three years," said De Waal.
Groups also praised the proposal to develop an early-warning system for food-related illnesses.

They noted the president was making his announcement almost four years to the day after a deadly outbreak of E coli bacteria in hamburgers cooked in fast food restaurants in the Pacific Northwest resulted in hundreds of people getting sick, and four deaths. Earlier warnings of that problem might have saved lives, consumer groups said.

U.S. agencies have been struggling to control persistent outbreaks of food-borne illnesses, including the deadly E coli bacteria from beef and salmonella from poultry, among others. The Agriculture Department this year is implementing a massive overhaul of its meat and poultry inspection system to cut down on the problems.
